name: Edgewonk
tagline: A trading journal that imports your trades and reports back on which habits are actually losing you money.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: A trading journal is a table of your own trades plus arithmetic on it. R-multiples, win rate by setup, expectancy, equity curve, time-of-day and day-of-week breakdowns, drawdown: all of that is a few SQL queries and a chart library, and none of it depends on anyone else's data. The genuinely annoying parts are broker CSV quirks, futures and options contract multipliers, and the discipline to log entries at all, and an agent can get you most of the way through the first two in a session. What you cannot generate is Edgewonk's opinionated set of metrics, which exist because someone spent years deciding which numbers make traders change behavior and which ones just look clever. Build it if you want your journal to live in a local SQLite file you control; buy it if you want the metrics chosen for you.
coreLoopDIY: Imports a broker CSV into a local SQLite trade log, tags each trade with setup and mistake labels, and renders expectancy, R-multiple distribution, equity curve and per-tag performance so you can see which behavior is bleeding money.
requirements: A CSV or Excel export of your trade history from your broker
Node 20 and the willingness to run a local dev server when you want to journal
whatYouLose: Prebuilt importers and column mappings for dozens of brokers, so every new account means another parser
The curated metric set and the explanations of why each number matters, which is most of what you are actually paying for
Simulation and what-if tooling, like replaying your history with a different stop or position size, unless you build it yourself
Screenshot attachment, tick-level trade replay and the mobile-friendly polish of logging on the go
Anyone to blame when your expectancy math is subtly wrong
moatNotes: The moat is pedagogy, not technology: knowing which six charts change trader behavior is harder than drawing sixty.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because the hard part of a trading journal was never the code, it was the structure. Edgewonk tells you which fields to fill in and which numbers to look at, and that opinionation is worth money to someone who has already stared at a blank spreadsheet for three months. There is also the uncomfortable fact that paying for a journal makes people more likely to actually use it, which no self-hosted app has ever solved.
notes: The arithmetic is trivial; deciding which arithmetic matters is the product.
prompt:
Build a local-first trading journal and analytics app. Single user, runs on my machine, no accounts, no cloud, no telemetry.

Stack, non negotiable:
- Next.js 14 App Router with TypeScript and Tailwind
- SQLite via better-sqlite3, file at ./data/journal.db, created and migrated on first boot
- Recharts for charts
- No auth, no external APIs, no analytics scripts

Data model:
- accounts: id, name, currency, starting_balance
- instruments: id, symbol, asset_class (stock, futures, forex, crypto, option), tick_size, point_value
- trades: id, account_id, instrument_id, direction (long/short), entry_time, exit_time, entry_price, exit_price, stop_price, size, fees, pnl_cash, r_multiple, setup, notes
- tags: id, name, kind (setup, mistake, emotion); trade_tags join table

Features in scope:
1. CSV import at /import: upload a file, show the first rows, let me map each CSV column to a trade field, save the mapping by name so reuse is one click. Handle both one-row-per-trade and separate entry/exit fill rows.
2. Manual trade entry form with the same fields.
3. Compute pnl_cash from price delta, size and point_value, and r_multiple from entry, stop and exit. Recompute on edit.
4. Dashboard: equity curve, cumulative R, win rate, average win vs average loss, expectancy per trade in R, profit factor, max drawdown, and a histogram of R outcomes.
5. Breakdown page: performance grouped by setup tag, mistake tag, instrument, day of week and hour of entry. Each group shows trade count, expectancy in R and total R. Sort by total R so the worst habits surface first.
6. Trade list with filters by date range, account, instrument and tag, plus inline edit and delete.
7. Export everything back to CSV and a one-click copy of the SQLite file.

Out of scope, do not build: broker API connections, live prices, multi user, charts of price action, screenshots, mobile app, anything that phones home.

Requirements: any secret or path config goes in .env.example with no real values. Seed the db with 40 fake trades behind a `npm run seed` script so the dashboard is not empty on first run. Write a README with setup in under ten lines and a short note on how r_multiple is calculated, including how it handles trades with no stop recorded.
